Tell them the order is split, track each box out loud, and warn them before the late one slips. Do that and a split order stays a fulfillment detail that never reaches your helpdesk. Key takeaways Last peak, 23% of shoppers had a package marked delivered that never arrived, according to Narvar + eTail Insights research. A split order produces the same panic when nothing is missing at all. Default shipped and delivered emails report on boxes, but shoppers think in orders. "I think it's lost" tickets start in the gap between the two. Four split shipment notifications close that gap: a split notice, per-box tracking, predictive delay alerts, and a delivery-anticipation email about 24 hours out. Jo Loves cut WISMO queries by 95% after moving past default Shopify notifications with Narvar Notify. Your shopper can’t tell late from lost A shopper orders a desk chair, a lamp, and a rug on a Monday in early December. The lamp and rug sit in one warehouse and the chair sits in another. So the order leaves as two parcels on two different days. Thursday afternoon, a box lands on the porch and an email arrives with "delivered" in the subject line. The shopper opens the box, finds a lamp and a rug, and looks for the chair. There is no chair. They reread the email. It still says delivered. Five minutes later, your team has a new ticket: "I think part of my order is lost." Nothing is lost. The chair is on a truck one day behind, exactly where your fulfillment plan put it. The shopper had no way to know that, so they did the only thing left to them. They asked a person. Multiply that exchange across every split order in peak and you get a helpdesk queue full of tickets about packages that were never missing. Want the full shopper data behind these numbers? We asked 1,348 shoppers what they want from brands this holiday season. Download the report. ‍ Two tracking numbers, one worried shopper A split shipment doubles the number of things that can go wrong in the shopper's eyes. Each box has its own carrier scans, its own delivery date, and its own chance to run late. But the shopper sees one order and one promise. Narvar's research shows how frequently a single box already breaks that promise. Narvar + eTail Insights’ Delivering the 2026 Holiday Shopping Season report surveyed 1,348 US shoppers and 100 retailers. Last peak, 37% of those shoppers had a package arrive late. Another 37% saw the delivery date change after they purchased. And 23% had a package marked delivered that never arrived. A split order runs two boxes through those odds. It also adds a failure of its own: a delivered email that's true for one box reads as false for the whole order. Our chair shopper files themselves under that 23%, even though the chair turns up a day later. (We broke down the questions shoppers ask between "shipped" and "delivered" in Why your support queue floods in December .) Retailers feel the pressure from their side, too. In the same report, 66% of retailers ranked on-time delivery as a top-three peak challenge. The pattern shows up in Narvar's sales conversations as well. One home furnishings retailer ships its products in several boxes. It described shoppers who opened the first delivery, started assembling a partial order, and assumed the rest had been stolen. Alerts for split shipments were its top reason for choosing Notify. 23% of holiday shoppers had a package marked delivered that never arrived. A split order recreates that moment even when every box is on its way. - Delivering the 2026 Holiday Shopping Season Default emails track boxes while shoppers track orders Most ecommerce platforms come with notifications built around two carrier events: shipped and delivered. Those two emails answer the shopper's easy questions and say nothing about the hard ones. A shipped email for box one doesn't mention that a second box exists. A delivered email doesn't say which items were inside, what's still coming, or when. When box two hits a carrier delay, nothing goes out at all, because "running late" isn't an event the default stack sends. Onia ran into exactly this. The swimwear brand was using Shopify's standard notification emails, and they couldn't keep up with how much its shoppers wanted to know. Onia's small team ended up fielding a stream of contacts from shoppers checking on their deliveries. After moving to Narvar, Onia cut WISMO by 18% . The emails that prevent tickets are the ones defaults don't send. Across Narvar Notify programs, predictive delay emails average a 38% click-through rate and attempted delivery emails average 34%. Delivered emails average just 8%. Shoppers open the message that tells them something changed, and that same message keeps them out of your queue. Four messages that keep a split order out of your helpdesk Keep splitting orders. Split shipments exist for good reasons: faster delivery, inventory spread across locations, items that ship from different partners. What changes is how much the shopper hears about each box, at each step, before they have to ask. 1. Announce the split in the first shipping email The first message after an order leaves should say plainly that it's coming in more than one package, and how many. We recommend a multi-shipment banner on the shipment confirmation for exactly this moment. A shopper who expects two boxes reads the first one as progress. A shopper who expects one reads it as a mistake. 2. Track every box on its own, and say what's in it Each tracking number gets its own updates. Narvar Notify follows every shipment in an order on its own schedule. Box one and box two each trigger their own on-its-way, delay, and delivered messages. Pair each message with the items inside that box: "Your lamp and rug were delivered today. Your chair arrives Friday." One sentence answers the ticket before anyone writes it. 3. blogs.author: Surabhi Gupta
blogs.content: How AI Redefined Engineering at Klaviyo Generated by Klaviyo AI Klaviyo made level 3 AI autonomy its engineering baseline, with agents implementing code while engineers define problems, set constraints, and remain accountable. The company measures impact through delivery, speed, quality, and hours saved while moving engineers closer to customer needs. Level 3 baseline: As of the end of July 2026, AI generated 85% of Klaviyo’s code under engineer-defined goals, constraints, and oversight. Judgment matters: Engineers increasingly focus on scoping problems, setting guardrails, and verifying whether AI-generated work should ship. Mixed experience: Teams combine junior engineers’ AI fluency with senior engineers’ experience in system design, decomposition, and verification. Sign up Get a demo Show AI generated summary On September 23, I joined Stephanie Cohen, Cloudflare ’s chief strategy officer, and Owen Jennings, Block ’s head of business, on a panel at The Information ’s AI Agenda Live in San Francisco. The event brought together leaders from OpenAI , Google DeepMind , NVIDIA , Atlassian , and EY to talk about where AI is gaining traction inside companies. On our panel, each of us described how our company has restructured around AI agents, and all of us concluded that AI works best when you redesign roles, decisions, and training around it. At Klaviyo, that redesign started with how we trained our own engineers. 4 levels of AI autonomy for engineering teams For us, the hardest problem was that the craft of engineering changed underneath people who’d spent a decade getting good at the old version of it. We gave our engineering team a framework, borrowed from how the industry talks about self-driving cars: Level 1: AI handles boilerplate and autocomplete. Level 2: Engineers delegate whole discrete tasks. Level 3: Engineers set the goal, the constraints, and the context up front, letting an AI agent write the implementation but staying fully accountable for what ships. Level 4: Engineers direct agents across large cross-system builds. We haven’t seen anyone do this reliably yet, because it needs stronger testing, observability, and self-correction than exists today. Level 3 is our baseline across Klaviyo today. As of the end of July 2026, 85% of our code was AI-generated. At level 3, engineers spend their time defining the problem, setting guardrails, and deciding whether what comes back is right. Andrew Bialecki, CEO of Klaviyo, discusses this shift in depth in his recent SaaStr interview . That same shift in judgment also changed how we evaluate talent. Engineers interviewing at Klaviyo now show us how they’d work with AI agents once they’re on the team. It also changed how we think about junior engineers. More than once on our panel, we heard that they still add value even though AI can generate so much code. Junior engineers are often AI native, so they start working at level 3 from day one. Senior engineers pick up these tools quickly too, and with their experience designing large systems and breaking work into the right pieces, they can become highly productive fast. Teams do well when they mix both, pairing fresh fluency with agents and deep judgment in scoping and verifying the work. How Klaviyo measures AI impact Everyone on the panel had seen engineering velocity climb, including pull requests and feature delivery. But shipping faster only helps if the feature was worth building in the first place. We track 4 numbers: how much we ship, how long it takes a change to reach customers, the quality of what ships, and how many hours we save across the teams we support. The fourth number comes from proximity. When engineers spend time alongside the teams they support, they find friction that no ticket captures, like hours lost to manual research before customer calls. Fixing that with AI has saved tens of thousands of hours across the organization. That’s why we put engineers closer to customers. At a growing company, requirements often pass through layers of people before they reach an engineer, so someone ends up picking up work without knowing why it matters. Any engineer should be able to explain, in their own words, why what they’re building is worth their time and which customer pain point it addresses. More of the building, by more builders More people and more agents are doing the building at Klaviyo. Our autonomous coding agent opens fixes for production errors on its own, and engineers decide what merges. We also built K:Forge, an internal platform on Vercel, and opened it to all employees. Some ideas go live in under 3 minutes, and in the first two weeks we shipped 356 apps , 196 of them full-stack with their own databases. With code this fast to write, the scarce skill is knowing which customer problem is worth solving. Engineers learn that by sitting close to customers and the teams that support them. If you’re redesigning your own engineering team, start there. Surabhi Gupta Surabhi Gupta has served as our Chief Technology Officer since September 2024. Prior to joining Klaviyo, Ms. Gupta served as Senior Vice President, Head of Engineering, from March 2022 to August 2023, as Vice President, Head of Engineering, from January 2021 to February 2022, and as Vice President, Product Engineering, from May 2020 to January 2021 at Robinhood Markets, Inc. (NASDAQ: HOOD), a financial services company. Ms. Gupta also served as Director of Engineering at Airbnb, Inc. (NASDAQ: ABNB), a software development company, from July 2013 to May 2020. Ms. Gupta currently serves as a board member of GetYourGuide Deutschland GmbH, a software development company. Ms. Gupta holds a Bachelor of Science degree from Stony Brook University and Master of Science, Computer Science from Stanford University. blogs.title: How Criquet Shirts Uses AI Segmentation to Send 40% Fewer Emails
blogs.author: Tracey Wallace
blogs.content: Fewer Sends, Higher Revenue Generated by Klaviyo AI Criquet Shirts used testing and AI-powered segmentation to target customers more precisely, reducing send volume by about 40% while increasing revenue 30% in the first 3 months. AI also helps its small team build segments and first drafts faster, while human judgment guides creative work and customer relationships. Test before pitching: Bucket tests gave leadership evidence that fewer, more targeted messages could outperform broader sending. Individual-level targeting: Klaviyo’s Orita integration scores customers using thousands of data points, including patterns that can identify seasonal shoppers. Measured business impact: The segmented approach cut send volume by about 40% and lifted revenue 30% in the first 3 months. AI saves time: Claude helps the small team build location-based segments and generate first drafts from existing briefs and product descriptions. Sign up Get a demo Show AI generated summary In 2010, two lifelong friends started apparel company Criquet Shirts in Austin, Texas, to pursue, in their words , “the perfect shirt and all things anti-ordinary.” So, it’s no surprise they hired former NFL mascot Zach Scheimer to lead retention marketing. Until recently, he ran the program alone before adding a junior team member. Scheimer’s approach to AI runs counter to the advice most marketers are hearing. Many company leaders are urging marketing teams to use AI to produce more emails, text messages, and content. But Scheimer uses AI to send fewer , more carefully targeted messages. His goal is a deeper relationship with each customer, and, in his experience, sending less, deliberately, can outperform sending more. Data on AI and trust gestures toward Scheimer’s instinct. According to Klaviyo's 2026 AI Consumer Trends Report , 32% of consumers say AI-generated marketing content makes them trust brands less. 61% are neutral, and only 7% say it increases trust. In our latest episode of Klaviyo Originals , Scheimer explains how he made the case for sending less during his career, how he uses AI segmentation to target audiences more precisely, where AI saves time, and which parts of the job remain human. How Scheimer used bucket tests to make the case for sending less Sending less can be a hard sell, especially to leaders who equate more sends with more revenue. Early in his career, Scheimer learned that a proposal to leadership goes further with evidence. Before his time at Criquet Shirts, Scheimer’s team was building a plain-text version of each email for BlackBerry users, with text variations for as many as 15 emails. Scheimer saw the work as wasted time, but he had no proof. So, he put a UTM parameter on each link in each text version. After a month, not one sale was directly attributable to those emails. "If you have a hypothesis you can test without breaking anything else,” Scheimer advises, “test it first, then go to leadership." Scheimer carried the learning experience to Criquet Shirts. Midway through last year, engagement was slowing and email deliverability was dropping. Before proposing a new strategy, he ran a bucket (A/B) test across email and text messages, grouping subscribers by engagement to see who was responding on a seasonal basis. "There are some customers who might not have clicked or opened an email in the last 180 days, but because of the seasonality, they’re still likely to buy," Scheimer explains. "So we knew with this bucket approach, we were missing people that were in a queue, wanting to hear from us." Early results from Scheimer’s bucket tests showed leadership that targeted messages could work, which opened the door to explore how AI could help him scale his segmented approach. How AI segmentation cut send volume 40% and lifted revenue 30% Before AI, Scheimer built and managed 15 segments based on his own knowledge of customers. He could message each of the 15 segments based on engagement within the last 180 days, but that approach missed seasonal shoppers, like customers who buy polos only in spring and summer. To reach seasonal shoppers, Criquet Shirts uses Klaviyo’s integration with Orita , a machine learning segmentation tool, to score each customer individually using thousands of data points. “It allows us to really scale that process and planning that we had done on the bucketed level, by being able to do it on the individual level,” Scheimer says. With this approach, the brand’s send volume dropped by about 40%, and revenue rose 30% in the first 3 months. “It was this massive change,” Scheimer points out. “I think starting with the bucketed approach and seeing small results from that helped leadership be like, ‘This is a working strategy. We can take this further.’ That's been huge for us.” The real value of AI: “You can save time for teams that don't have time” Scheimer defines AI narrowly. "Not everything is AI," he says. "AI, to me at least, is more agentic.” For him, that means "using Claude to help automate processes," especially ones that used to take him hours. Last Father's Day, Scheimer put AI workflows to the test. To generate in-store revenue, he wanted to send a hyper-targeted email with a specific goal: to make sure last-minute shoppers could buy Criquet Shirts products in stores if they couldn't order online in time. So, Scheimer used Claude to quickly set up segments of subscribers within 15 miles of the 215 retail locations that carry their products. The task took 30 minutes as he learned how to prompt Claude, but, for a later collegiate product launch, a similar segment took 10–15 minutes to build. "That's where I see the real value in AI: you can save time for these teams that don't have time,” Scheimer explains. “That's their most precious resource as a team." “AI gets you to step one”: Criquet Shirts’ AI writing philosophy Two copywriters have left Criquet Shirts during Scheimer's time there, partly because a business of their size doesn't consistently have enough work for one. So, Scheimer’s team started training a copywriting skill in Claude. “We've used Google Docs for 6 years for all of our email and text message briefs,” Scheimer explains. “We can now feed that into Claude. Claude also has access to Shopify, where all of our product descriptions are, and can pull from those.” “So, instead of me spending 10–20 minutes pulling from last time we wrote a similar email, I can have Claude spit out a first draft, and I can make edits,” Scheimer adds. Shoppers are split on AI-written messages. Globally, 57% of consumers assume most brand messages are AI-generated, according to Klaviyo's 2026 State of the Holiday Buyer Report . Just under half say AI-written messages bother them, while 55% don't mind as long as the message is helpful and relevant. Scheimer is clear about where the role of AI ends. "I don't think AI is great at creative, whether it's imagery or writing,” he says. “I think it gets you to step one and takes away some of the writer's block phase, where it gives you a first draft and then you can actually write from there." How gift buyers changed Criquet Shirts’ email send frequency For Scheimer, the whole point of sending less with AI is to deepen the brand relationship with each customer. That means taking customer feedback seriously throughout the entire lifecycle. For example, when one shopper said they wanted all of the campaigns and none of “the flow messages,” specifically abandoned cart reminders , Scheimer checked the customer’s profile . Sure enough, he could see they weren't engaging with flows, so he added a suppression to each flow for that one person. It was something he didn't expect to repeat for any other customer, but he took the request as a starting point for further investigation.
